speechtext:
I beg your pardon,
Mr. Speaker, for the oversight. The right hon. leader of the Opposition received his answer when he appealed to the people. Instead of a following of something like 125 members his supporters now number barely 50. During the election the right hon. gentleman's cohorts went to the province of Quebec telling the people that they would have empty dinner pails if they voted against the Meighen Government. In my own county are two or three of the largest industries in the Dominion. Representatives of these industries went about telling the working men that if they did not vote for the Meighen Government those industries would be closed down. The Dominion Textile Company is one of the industries in question, and although I do not think the management of that company meddles in politics, certain emissaries went up and down making all sorts of predictions as to what would happen unless the working classes voted right. The Union Twist Drill Company is another concern with a capitalization of three million dollars. The day before the election notice was posted up on its premises that the factory would close close down if the employees did not vote for the Meighen Government. In Compton County, the night before the election, seventeen of the local returning officers were dismissed and replaced by men from Montreal and other points and as a result of their nefarious work 1,500 ballots were destroyed. These are some of the means by which support was sought for the Meighen Government. The right hon. leader of the Opposition and the late Minister of Marine, Mr. Ballan-tyne, toured the Eastern Townships but their efforts were not very successful. The Meighen candidate in Stanstead lost his deposit by more than 700 votes and I want to tell my right hon. friend that had he been the candidate he would have suffered
The Address

a similar defeat. Neither the high protection talk nor the scandal that was sought to be disseminated had any influence against the Liberals in the province of Quebec. Although the leader of the Opposition has sneered at the Premier's following from that province I beg to assure him that in admitting the ex-Premier and the ex-Treasurer of Quebec to the Cabinet he has chosen men of eminence who will be of great assistance to the Government and the country. I want to tell the hon. gentleman, the minister sitting at the right of the Prime Minister, that there is one thing firmly established in this country, and that is the great Liberal party. Liberalism means just what it says. It means Charity, a willingness to rely on the people and the people's judgment, to obey the will of the country. It does things with an eye to the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood of God. It does business with an eye to the poor and the oppressed. It has a kindly feeling for the poor people. It has an eye to the great agriculturalists of whom the leader of the Agrarians (Mr. Crerar) has spoken. The right hon. leader of the Opposition and his party likened the Agrarians to Bolshevists, and I take umbrage at the accusation. I may say that I have worked fifteen hours a day and thrived on it, and I think any man who endeavours to injure the toiler of the land is making a great mistake. I want to tell the leader of the Opposition that he will never lead the government of Canada again unless he disassociates himself from the autocrats, the plutocrats, the stiff-necked chest-padded militarists of the country, who wish to domineer and dominate everything and to separate themselves from the tillers of the soil. The people trusted the former government too long, and I may tell you that you cannot force people into doing things. The former government, while not characterized as kaiserism, was indeed kaiserism, without any mistake. The leader of the Opposition has come into this House. Having been defeated in -his own constituency, he was enabled to come here by a charitable act, a gentleman being persuaded to retire in his favour, and I suppose he gave him a good figure for it. We know that he is getting in his position a good sum of money, and when he comes here he has to assail somebody, but when he assails such men as he did yesterday, he is not winning any votes. He is not intimidating the people who are in the Government now because we 
are proud of them and the country is proud of them.
I assure him that we have many things to do in this country without fighting each other. We have great potential wealth, and we have a vast country. Let us talk in this House as we would like it to appear in Hansard in future generations. The leader of the Agrarian party was provoked to say in the last days of the last parliament, that the leader of the then government was a vendor of cheap political vaudeville. Likewise the hon. member for Russell and now Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) characterized him as the sluggoo of the Borden government. This young man no doubt has aspirations and I can see that he has reason. Eight or ten years ago, when people came to Ottawa they returned to their homes and said that the whole brains of the government was in Robert Rogers. I think that was humiliating to a young man who was cultured and able and would make a good critic in this House. He was jealous of the superior brain power that had been attributed to Rogers as compared with that of his fellow members of the Conservative party. We know that Mr. Rogers was the champion of Sir Robert Borden when he went overseas, and came back to put through the Conscription Bill. Mr. Rogers said "We must get something to win the election, and conscription may do it". They were out not to win the war, but to win the election, and it cost the country a vast amount of money to put that machinery into force.
I would not want to talk on the lines of the leader of the Opposition. We have a great country; we want the members of this House to deal with affairs in a businesslike way and we do not want the time of this House wasted on other matters. I would not have spoken except for the accusation of being one of the cohorts and I am sure there are other members in the House in the same position. I am proud to be a follower of the leader of the Government. They are kindly hearted gentlemen who can smile and smile for humanity's sake. They feel for the people and their hearts beat for the poor and the oppressed. They feel for the masses of this country. They do not believe in doing things by might but wish to do things by right.
I will not take up more time in this House but I recommend the leader of the Opposition to take the Decalogue and the

The Address
Sermon on the Mount as a chart and compass for his future life.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to be as brief as I possibly can in addressing the House, and to that end I have taken the liberty of taking a seat in the middle of the House so that I can he heard by hon. gentlemen opposite and by hon. gentlemen on either side of me, because I want to follow the example of the hon. leader of the Progressives in the House (Mr. Crerar), and devote myself to at least one of the most important questions now before the people of Canada. So determined am I to devote my time to the discussion of this question that I must forego the example set by the hon. gentlemen who preceded me, leave it to others to pay the compliments which have been paid to yourself and to hon. gentlemen who have spoken and give my time to the question that I propose to bring before you. I have every appreciation of the honour that has been done to you. I have every appreciation of the speeches of the mover and seconder. I am glad to see the lady member in the House. I shall pass other compliments, and come directly to the railway question to which the leader of Progressives devoted most of his time.
I come here, not for the first time, as one who is an absolute believer in public ownership of public utilities. I have been connected with that movement in regard to municipal and provincial affairs, and in regard to the railways and other public utilities of the country. I come from a city which to-day has the finest example of public ownership of a public utility in the street railway system of Toronto, run by the Transportation Commission appointed by the people to run the people's own road for the benefit of the people. It embodies the essential principle of public ownership, namely, that once the people own a utility, they are free to do with it what they like, whenever they like, even if their action sometimes involves, as it did recently, an increase in fares. Toronto to-day has the finest street car service in America-I say that after careful consideration-and while at present we have a seven-cent fare, the street railway is doing so well and is accumulating such reserves that the fare will soon be five cents and later on four cents, and, I think we may yet come back to the "eight tickets for a quarter."
We have something else to show in Ontario in the nature of a public utility owned by the people, and that is the magnificent
hydro-electrical development, best exemplified by its most recent instance, that of the Chippewa hydro-electrical development in connection with the Niagara river. Sir Adam Beck has been attacked; but he has made good; he is delivering the power, and the greatest electrical development in the world to-day is owned by the people of Ontario at this new power plant on the Niagara river. Only the first generator has been started; but another will be started tomorrow and each of them will deliver 55,000 h.p. The development of power may reach as much as 600,000 h.p.; it may reach 1,000,000 h.p., and the income from that may be from five to ten million dollars. This development has not had an opportunity yet to show what can be accomplished; but it has been very severely criticised, and Sir Adam Beck has been held up to the people of Canada, even by the United Farmers' Government of Ontario, as one who has been rather loose in his estimates of the cost of establishing this hydro-electric plant. I just want to ask my friend Mr. Drury, Premier of Ontario-and I have a great deal of respect for him-when he speaks about Sir Adam Beck exceeding his estimates, what about his own treasurer and the financial statement which he has brought down to the Legislative Assembly? I want to ask my friends here from the West- and I have a great deal of sympathy with their ideas, as I will show later on-what about the good roads that have been built in Ontario by the Hon. Mr. Biggs? He was to give us the cheapest and best kind of good roads throughout Ontario and to keep well within his estimates. We thought we were going to get roads for at most $2,000, or $3,000, a mile, some for $10,000 and, perhaps, a few at $20,000 a mile, but some of them have cost nearly $100,000 a mile. When criticism is being made in Ontario in regard to Sir Adam Beck's estimates for the construction of the hydroelectric plant, that criticism, if it is to be fair, must be common to all the public men of Ontario. Therefore, I say here to-day that I am proud of Sir Adam Beck and what he has done in the direction of public ownership. He has given to all the world the greatest example of the production of electrical power for the welfare of the people, the sole idea being service and not profit.
The great difference between public ownership and private ownership is that in public ownership-and this applies to railways which is the main question that
The Address

I am going to discuss to-day-the principal object in view on the part of the men administering the public utility, after paying necessary interest, is service and not profits. Heretofore the great object of the executive administering a public utility has been profits for the owners and the stockholders; but the idea in public ownership, as illustrated by Sir Adam Beck, is service at a low cost. Notwithstanding the criticism that has come from Montreal about Sir Adam Beck's proposition and his public power distribution, we have the cheapest and best service of that kind in Canada. There is nothing to equal it. I see by recent legislation that the consolidation of the power interests in Montreal is to furnish 300,000 h.p., but we in Ontario-and mainly by the leadership of the municipalities by Sir Adam Beck-will soon have over 1,000,000 h.p., and we are going to put that electrical energy into the home of every farmer in Ontario. That is what we have in view; we are working it out, and there is fair support coming from the Legislature in that direction.
Therefore, public ownership of public utilities is nothing new to us in Ontario; we are succeeding in it, and we believe in that public ownership being extended to the railway systems of Canada. We do so for several reasons, one being that we have come into possession of all these so-called bankrupt railways, because of bad administration by the companies that had them and also probably because the country was overbuilt with railways. Now that we are in possession of them, we propose to try public ownership of these publicly-owned railways in the interest of the people and outside of the question of dividends for the shareholders who formerly owned them. We came into possession of these railways, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, because they were not very well administered by those who had control of them. Why did the Grand Trunk fail? It failed because, while it was owned largely in Great Britain, it was administered in London. You cannot run a Canadian railway from London; it must be administered in this country. The Grand Trunk would have been a success ten, twenty years ago, if it had been administered absolutely in Canada; but it was run from London and run by directors whose main object, so far as I can gather-and I have followed my investigations rather deeply-was to play the London stock market in Grand Trunk securities. That is one reason why

the Grand Trunk has failed. The Grand Trunk, to my mind, is one of the greatest railway assets in America-and I speak after careful consideration-and it is the greatest railway asset in Canada. When you look at the strategic positions that the Grand Trunk has in this country, at Montreal, at Ottawa, along the St. Lawrence, at Toronto, London, Detroit, along the Niagara river and throughout the province of Ontario, and when you consider all the branch lines connected with it, it must be admitted it is the greatest railway asset in America.
It is undoubtedly the best road we have in Canada, and all it requires is good management. With a proper Canadian directorate it would prove a wonderful success, and it is just because it is likely to be a great success that we find the Canadian Pacific, with its headquarters in Montreal, endeavouring to head it off. I think I can see the hand of the Canadian Pacific, and that of its close associate, the Bank of Montreal, joined together in an effort to thwart the Grand Trunk, which is a real rival. What is the source of the inspiration of all this talk that we see in the Montreal papers and in some of the papers in the province of Ontario? This agitation does not come from the people or from the men who work on the roads; nor does it originate with the people who use the railways. No, it comes largely from the city of Montreal, whose newspapers seem to talk of nothing else but the Canadian Pacific railway. I have nothing to say against that railway; it is the one Canadian railway that has been a success. But it has one peculiar clause in its charter, whereby the company is bound to maintain a railway service forever. That obligation has never been imposed on any other road, but it has been imposed on the Canadian Pacific railway for a purpose, and that is, that the public shall always be assured of a service of some kind. The Canadian Pacific Railway is the creature of this Parliament and of the people of Canada. We have created it and given it the charter it holds, involving great powers. We gave it some $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 at the start, in addition to some 25,000,000 acres of land, and it has had all kinds of friendly legislation put through this House in its behalf. Altogether it has been well treated not only by Parliament but as well, by the municipalities throughout the country.
This railway, on which is imposed the responsibility of providing the people of

The Address
Canada with a service for all time, now turns against Parliament, its creator, and against the people of the country, and says: "Don't you dare to start national railways in this country or we will destroy you." That is the attitude of the Canadian Pacific railway and its friends in Montreal. They simply defy the people of Canada who created them, and warn us that we shall embark on public ownership of railways in this country only at our own peril. They tell us that public ownership is bad for the country, and that if we do not abandon the idea we shall suffer. Talking about the Canadian Pacific railway and the question of public ownership, and in connection with the references that have been made to Sir Adam Beck, there is not a radial proposition that Sir Adam Beck has started which has not been denounced by these enemies of his, and yet which would not be taken over to-morrow by President Beatty of the Canadian Pacific railway. That gentle* man knows all about them, and he would take over every radial and be glad to go to Sir Adam Beck for his power. And he will soon have to do so, because it will be necessary to have power to run the Canadian Pacific railway, and we shall have enough power in Ontario to operate every railway train from Detroit down to Ottawa. We shall soon have that power to sell outside the country, and I hope that Quebec will have a large share. That aside, however, I want to come back to the subject with which I was dealing a moment ago.
The Canadian Pacific railway, created by the Parliament and the people of Canada, now tells us, in the coun-5 p.m. try and in this House, that we must not embark on public ownership of the railways that we have. If we heed that command, what will ensue? Let me point out to the Prime Minister that if we allow the Canadian Pacific railway to put the Canadian National railway out of business, if we stand by and let Montreal dictate to us in this matter, we shall have created the greatest political tyranny that ever existed in any country, because the Canadian Pacific railway hopes to have every road in Canada, and the Montreal Gazette already informs us that we cannot run the Canadian National railways and therefore urges us to turn them over to the Canadian Pacific. What would happen if the Canadian Pacific railway got the National railway? Could any one of us remain in politics? Would any man have
a chance of getting into this House, into any provincial legislature, or into any municipal council, with the Canadian Pacific railway owning all the railroads of the country-the great political boss of the country being in Montreal, with a subordinate boss in every town and village acting as local agent of the Canadian Pacific railway? Why, Sir, political independence would cease in this country if we created such a tyranny. Yet that is the object of this great movement against public ownership of our railways.
And how is the tyranny entrenched, so far as it has gone? It has been entrenched, so far, by a marvellous device known as the "Voting Trust." I do not know whether hon. gentlemen know what a voting trust is, but I have some idea of what it signifies, and as a splendid example I might mention a weil'l-known mine in Ontario, of which sixty to seventy per cent is controlled by certain relatives. This property has been entailed, so that this mine in the future may never be interfered with, no matter what may befall the families that owned it originally. That, perhaps, is fairly within their rights; but when you entail the administration of a railway that -has the political ambitions of the Canadian Pacific railway, with its railway monopoly, and an arrangement whereby only two of * their board retire each year, there being a concentration of shareholders on the election of these two, I say you are entrenching a tyranny. The object of these men now established in the control of the Canadian Pacific railway is to retain that control, get possession of the other railways, and thereby become the great and only political boss of transportation in the country, and, incidentally, of the people's legislation as well.
Now, I appeal to hon. gentlemen in this House, whether opposite or on either side of me: are we, the people's representatives in Parliament, to assist the Canadian Pacific railway in acquiring all the railways of the country, simply because they warn us that, if we dare to administer our own roads, which have come into our hands as a result of the failures of those who had charge of them, we shall be put out of business? These railways that we have were forced upon us, and enormous sums of the people's money have been- put into them. Is it fair that this creature of the Canadian Parliament should take that position, which I am led to believe they have already taken?

The Address

I am not antagonistic to the Canadian Pacific railway. I give them credit for what they have done. The road is a well administered one, with a good executive and good equipment, and they have done a good deal for the settlement of the country. But that is their business; let them devote their attention to it. Now that we are going to run these roads as a national proposition we will ask them to co-operate with us in the work of consolidation which I trust the Government intends to embark upon. I do not wish to antagonize the Canadian Pacific. But in connection with this matter of consolidation, it is to be noted that in the city of Toronto, for instance, all the traffic that comes, say, from Chicago has to go up a one per cent grade; and the same applies to the Canadian Pacific with its Wexford grade. Now that we have public ownership it is possible to build a line across Toronto in connection with the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways that will reduce that grade of one per cent down to half of one per cent and by that means alone bring about a saving of hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. If the Canadian Pacific want the use of our national railways for some consideration that they will give-and I know they will give something towards it-we can give them something to help in the solution of these transportation problems; for if we have public ownership we shall be willing to work with them. We do not wish to put them out of business, but they wish to put the people of Canada out of business so far as the competition of the national railways is concerned.
I think the Canadian Pacific will be well advised, and the Bank of Montreal will be well advised if they devote their attention to working out the destinies of the Canadian Pacific railway as an entity in this country, competing with the national railways, setting a pace for the national railways, if you like. They are welcome to do that, but they are not to be allowed to achieve their ambition of taking over the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National and the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Intercolonial. They would take these roads all into their maw, but on what terms? Will the Montreal Gazette tell us on what terms? Will any gentleman in the Government who has given some attention to the claims of the Canadian Pacific tell us on what terms? Do you think they would take them over

for nothing? No; they would want also a sum at least equivalent to the deficits that these roads are now sustaining. They may say: Give us what you gave to the losing concerns and perhaps we will run these roads for you. It is true that they may now modify their offer; they want to get these roads because they think they are good business propositions. But we should keep them for ourselves and operate them for the solution of Canada's transportation problems.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Now then, I am going to ask the Prime Minister and I am going to ask the leader of the Progressive party in this House what they mean by co-ordination. It is a very nice word; but what the leader of the Progressive party was talking about-I notice that he is not in the Chamber at the moment-was consolidation, and that is my word. Co-ordination as affecting railway lines is putting half a dozen companies together, retaining all their separate presidents and officials and separate equipment, and keeping them bucking one against the other. I do not think the leader of the Progressive party means that; in fact a little later in his remarks he said it was consolidation into one system that he was thinking of. When the Prime Minister uses the word co-ordination, does he mean that there will be real consolidation and actual elimination of unnecessary duplications? As we have the national railways now there are several presidents, all kinds of operating chiefs, all kinds of stations everywhere, and there are a whole lot of unnecessary lines. If you want to solve the transportation problem there must be consolidation and it has got to start now. The Prime Minister intimates that as he has just come into office he wants investigation. Well, he has a first-class railway department; he has expert railway men in the service of these different companies who can give him tomorrow any advice he may require with regard to the consolidation that ought to take place. In fact, legislation has already been passed for the consolidation of these roads and can be made effective to-morrow. So that it is real consolidation I wish to see, not co-ordination in the ordinary sense of the word-and I am glad that the leader of the Progressive party does not so construe it.
Public ownership is regarded by its opponents in this country as something very bad, as something which has failed. But the real fact is-and it has been demonstrated by experience throughout the whole of this continent-that company-owned and corporation-owned railways have failed, and that is what I wish to impress upon hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly those who are members of the Government. They cannot give a single instance where corporation ownership of railroads has succeeded in the United States. That it has failed all along the line I shall prove in a few minutes by the
statements of the chief enemies of public ownership of the American roads,- because they have been very busy of late. Because of the failure of company-owned railways in the United States the roads were taken over by the Federal authorities for war purposes and were given billions of national money in order that they might be put on their feet for the service of the nation. They took that money and lost it, and now they are preparing a most awful bill of charges for submission to Congress, said to be based upon losses sustained by the roads while under Government administration during the war. So that corporation-owned railways in the United States, which have been referred to by some hon. gentlemen in their arguments against public ownership, have fallen down worse than have the corporation-owned roads in Canada. They have as I shall show, more unnecessary duplication in connection with the American roads than we have in Canada.
To show how badly they have fallen down, I am going to quote briefly one or two things that come from the railways themselves. The American roads have seen for many years what was coming, and they have prepared themselves. They are thoroughly organized; they have got possession of very influential papers in the United States. The most outstanding defender of corporation-owned roads on this continent to-day is the Saturday Evening Post, published in Philadelphia. It is a paper that appeals to all classes of the public, although it is specially devoted now to an appeal to the women and to social ideas. It has a great run of advertising and mixed up with its articles on the railway situation are pictures of handsome young women in short skirts and silk stockings. There are many hosiery advertisements in the paper, but the main purpose of the Saturday Evening Post-and I say it on my full responsibility-a paper that has more influence on public opinion, or thinks it has, probably than any other paper in the United States, is to save the corporation-owned railroads of the United States from the doom that is coming to them. The corporation roads over there have failed. How do I know they have failed? The Saturday Evening Post has assigned to a very competent writer, Mr. Herbert Quick, the writing of a series of articles on "America, An Experiment in. Transportation." The first article has a great deal in it, but I am going to read only two or three extracts
The Address

from it. Mr. Herbert Quick, the best man they have been able to put forward in defence of the corporation-owned roads, admits that the roads have been a failure, and he says they cannot be put on their feet unless two things are done-the hundreds of comparatively small railroads they have in the United States must be consolidated into twelve systems, at the most, for purposes of economy, and it will require, so he says, at least four billions of the money of the people of the United States to be placed immediately at the disposal of these companies that have failed over there. That is rather an astounding thing to come in a discussion of this kind when we are warned as a people to beware of state-owned roads. It shows what a mess the corporation-owned roads in the United States have made of themselves.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why did it take so long to co-ordinate the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific with the National Railways? The Drayton-Acworth Report recommended that nearly four years ago.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I could coordinate them to-morrow successfully. There are lots of railway men in this country who could do it. The question is how slow the process is to be, whether there is to be acceleration or whether there is to be great delay, and while you are delaying you are giving the Canadian Pacific Railway a chance to lay all its plans for the bedevilment of the thing when it comes on. That is why they want coordination instead of consolidation.
Let me read what Mr. Herbert Quick says as to this great corporation-owned systems in the United States that are being held up to the Canadian people as an example for us to follow:
We as a nation have wagered our very existence on it-
That is, on the success of the railways over there.
We bet our life on the fact that an agency

That is, the railways.
-an agency, not one-tenth as economical as the water transport, which the human race for thousands of years had depended upon as the basis of every complex communal life. ...could hear the burden of all the tonnage that the multiplying population could create in the heart of a continent in a new era when human wants would grow by what they fed on.
And his finding is that the railways have failed, after having dispossessed the country of the water transportation facilities they had, that they are in an awful mess

financially, that the service is bad, and that the rates are high. The whole case of the farmers of the Western United States is the same as the farmers of our West-the exorbitant railway rates of these corporation-owned roads that have failed. Mr. Quick goes on to say:
We bet our national life on that, and we built our nation in the confident expectation that we should win.
That is by the railways.
It was the nerviest gamble of all history. It will take a long time to tell whether or not we have won it. He who is sure that we have won is over-optimistic.
That is the opinion of the best spokesman and the most expensive spokesman they have from the newspaper point of view. He says that he is over-optimistic who thinks that the transportation system of the United States has succeeded. The United States has become a great country; they have roads from the Atlantic across the plains to the Pacific, but as this writer points out, they have destroyed inland water transport; they have put several canals out of business and after having done all that, this writer says that he is an over-optimistic man who says that the corporation-owned railways of the United States are solving the transportation problems of that country. There are dozens of other arguments in this article in the Saturday Evening Post of February 25, and in the succeeding article in the issue of March 4, in which this writer admits the whole thing. I ask hon. gentlemen who do not wish to take my word for it to read for themselves these articles by this special writer in this specially friendly newspaper to the corporation-owned railways of the United States, in which it is shown that the corporation-owned roads over there have failed to solve the transportation problems of that country.
Now I want to get away from the weeklies of the United States and to read what is said in a prominent monthly in that country, the Century Magazine. It has had a series of articles on the railway question in the United States, and in its issue for March asks the question; What is the matter with the railroads? That is a problem that has presented itself to this leading magazine. The article from which I am about to quote appears in this month's issue and can be found in the library by any hon. member who wishes to read it. Here is how the writer concludes his article:

The Address
The sole alternatives to private ownership and operation are Government ownership and operation. To the majority of Americans the very idea of a further governmental control is extremely distasteful, to put the matter mildly. To them it is a very real menace. Yet the menace cannot be avoided by merely singing a song of hate about it. It can be overcome and finally prevented only by some definite national plan or policy in regard to our roads, a simple thing in which for a number of years we have been sadly lacking. If such a plan means their radical re-organization, we must begin, and the sooner the better.
The railroads have to be reorganized in the United States in the opinion of this writer in the "Century Magazine" and, he says, the sooner they begin the better. Are we encouraged then to continue that system here in Canada, or are we not justified in trying to recover our position and to see what the State can do rather than what the private corporations can do in the way of public transportation? Just to show how serious the situation is and how much the transportation problem is involved in it, let me say that the same magazine has another article by Alleyne Ireland entitled " Democracy and the Human Equation." His article is devoted to the subject: Can we save constitutional government? Let me read a few words from what he says as to what is the case in the United States and is also probably the case in Canada:
Constitutional government is to-day menaced by a serious and world-wide dissatisfaction with the operation of existing political institutions. We are confronted not only by the various forms of protest, adopted by those who wish to destroy existing institutions of Government, but also by a growing sense of helplessness and exasperation among those who wish to preserve them. There is scarcely a country in the world in which public discontent with the inefficiency and with the extravagance of government has not reached the danger point.
The plain fact is that for more than a hundred years the constitutionalists in every country have been issuing and constantly renewing promissory notes for human betterment, and that the further renewal of these notes is becoming increasingly difficult.
Then the writer goes on to point out what a marvellous change has been effected in the general conditions of human life, and how all that was promised in these respects has been delivered. In the case of transportation no relief has been delivered, and the Constitutionalists do not know where to go, and that is one of the questions that concerns this writer. He asserts that the railway question is coming up in United States and it has to be settled. According to Mr. Herbert Quick four billions more of public money, a reduction of the systems to twelve and electrification are required. Mr. Quick is out for electrification, but he wants that electrification to be done by private interests.
Now I might rest my case there, as to the failure of corporation-owned railways in the United States, on the authority of the witnesses I have cited, but you can bring hundreds more of them together to bear out what I say in regard to corporation-owned railways-that they have failed in the United States and cannot be redeemed except by the expenditure of billions of public money. But the corporations over there do not likepublicownership. They want the railroads to be given to them and compensation for their administration: "Give us more money and let us run them. We will see you are charged enough freight rates, but let us run them." Now that situation has come to the United States, and I think it has come to the people in Canada. We have the roads now. Shall we try public ownership and shall we give it a fair trial? Shall that trial, in the first instance be "a consolidation" and not this more doubtful proceeding

"a co-ordination of companies." Is that what is meant by co-ordination or does it mean consolidation? I only wish the leader of the Progressive party were here now to tell me. I did not wish to interrupt him when he was speaking but if he were here he could give us a definition of a term he was constantly using, the term "co-ordination." The really important word is "consolidation" as provided by the existing statutes of Canada and I hope developments will be in that direction.	.
Now I want to go another step in discussing whether corporation-owned railways in the United States have failed, and I would like to cite another witness. President Harding made a deliverance in the United States in regard to transportation in that country. If you ask me what his deliverance was, it was that we must get back to the water-ways. The railroads had not paid and they had overcharged the farmers. He had been waited on by a most important political delegation, the so-called farmers' bloc in Washington, and the President of the United States had to admit that the corporation-owned railroads had failed. They have destroyed water transportation and the improvement of the transportation problem is to get back to the rivers, back to water transportation, better still back to the introduction of sea-going vessels to the great lakes of Canada and of the United States. This involves mak-
The Address

ing seaports on our lakes. Make Toronto a seaport as well as Montreal. Perhaps the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) will not like that, but President Harding says:	Have seaports in Lake Ontario;
have them at Toronto and at Buffalo. Have them in Lakd Erie at Cleveland and at Port Stanley, and our other harbours on the north shore. Have them in Lake Huron. Have them in Lake Michigan, and make Chicago and Milwaukee seaports. It will not cost a great deal of money for we have had the finding of the International Joint Commission on it. President Harding advocates that we make ocean ports in Lake Superior so that the grain of the western States as well as the grain of the Canadian West may be loaded into seagoing vessels on those lakes. Resort to canalization if necessary, and at the same time develop water-power to take the place of coal which is owned by the greatest monopoly in America. Let the waterpower he developed for the betterment of railway transportation. Now that is a pretty good witness to call against corporation-owned railways. I am citing now a recent delivery of the President of the United States, to the effect that he is in favour of developing this water power and using it for the electrification of the. railways.
But there has turned up in Washington within the last two or three years a new political force, and it is turning up here in Canada now. There are 65 gentlemen in the Parliament of Canada to speak for the farmers of the Canadian West. I am glad to see them, and I hope they will speak out as their leader did to-day. I have nothing against the farmers. They have the cause of Canada in regard to transportation at heart. But what about your fellows in the United States? Do you know that the farmers in the United States, this so-called bloc, control thirty-five of the senators in that country, and any day they are asked to stand up for the farmers' interest they do so. This so-called farmers' bloc in the United States know that the great corporation-owned railways of the United States have failed. They have asked the President for relief, and they are now putting themselves on record as believing that the only relief they can give to the farmers of the United States must come through public ownership, waterways and the generation of electrical energy, to take the place of the coal monopoly in the United States.

Let me give an outstanding illustration of what transportation by sea-going vessels means compared to railways, and a wonderful illustration has come out recently in the United States. They spent millions of dollars in the development of the fisheries of Alaska, and the herring fisheries in Alaska are the equal of any in the world, but do you know what it cost to take a barrel of herring from Alaska to New York by rail? It cost $5 a barrel to take it to New York for distribution to the farmers of the United States in the eastern section where there is a large consumption of fish. A man went into a store to buy some of these fish, and inquired, " How much are they worth a barrel?" the merchant- answered " So much, plus $5 for transportation." The gentleman went into another fish store, and asked the price of a barrel of herring, and was quoted a much lower figure. He said, "How can you get them so much cheaper than another dealer?" He says, " We can get all herring caught in the fisheries of Scotland delivered into New York at 50 cents a barrel." That is 50 cents a barrel as against $5 a barrel for fish sent from Alaska. Has not the President of the United States some reason for finding that corporation-owned railways have failed? Have not the farmers of the United States some reason for coming back to the waterways and government control of railways, rather than that corporation control should continue?
Now the farmers of the United States are demanding relief and our farmers here are demanding relief. I believe that the whole of the farmers, not only of Western Canada, but the farmers of Ontario, are demanding relief. We have our transportation problem. We have high traffic charges and have to meet them. If there can be an improvement by improved canalization, by generation of electrical energy in connection with the canalization and the river powers we have, why not take them over? But the province of Quebec says "Oh, you in Ontario, must not generate public power, and you must' not be a party to co-operating with the United States in generating public power. You must cease doing that." But we say we do intend to generate that power as the United States are doing, and we intend to use it for the electrification of railways.
Let me speak about the electrification of railways. We have spent, I do not know how much, in the way of bringing American coal into this country to run our rail-

ways. Why not run our railways by the electrical service supplied by water-power on our Canadian rivers? In Ontario we have more than we need. The Niagara and St. Lawrence will move every train from Detroit to away below Quebec. Right here to the south of us, on the Ontario side we have the St. Lawrence river at .Cornwall, with a possibility of development there near Cornwall island. About 6 or 8 or 12 years ago a very rich and influential American company called the Aluminum Company came to us in the Railway Committee, and asked us to give them a charter to take over that great water-power on the St. Lawrence near Cornwall. They pretty nearly had it, but we made opposition to it and we have it now. There is enough power in the St. Lawrence in front of us here, in the Niagara river and in the Ottawa river to run every train in Canada from the Atlantic clean up to Port Arthur, and there are wonderful powers west of Port Arthur on the Saskatchewan that can be developed. We have had fine engineers in this country who have advocated the canalization of our country from lake Superior to the foot of the Rocky mountains, and that may be one of your great reliefs in the West. You will get abundance of water-power there to move your traffic. And why do they fear-why does the Canadian Pacific Railway fear- the electrification of railways? A new instrument is put in the hands of the people, when they control the water-power and the electrical energy, and I believe that is what President Harding has in view. That is what we have in view in this country-that if the country controls the water-power that runs the railway, and if a corporation road has to buy it- and I hope the Canadian Pacific Railway will be one of those-we will be able to put the blocks to them, to use a rough term, and we will be able to make them treat the public fairly. Who owns the coal of the United States that we have had to pay such a high price for? It is owned by the railways. They control the coal supply of the United States largely, and they want to control our water-powers. This Aluminum Company, one of the greatest metal trusts in the world, was in Ottawa a few years ago, and tried to grab the water-powers on the St. Lawrence, and the Prime Minister of Quebec says "Oh, I have a great dread of the Americans coming into our country and getting hold of our water-powers. I do not want to see them get
them." But I know that if the President and men like the President get some of that electrical energy generated by that water-power, it will be used fairly. I am not afraid of what he will do with these powers. He will use them fairly. But the province of Quebec says "No, we do not want the President of the United States to invade this country. We do not believe in public ownership." 'Still they have taken over the liquor business, and are going to pay $10,000,000 of their debt by the profits from it. Perhaps they had better try to develop the water-powers of Quebec. That province is rich in water-powers, and they have been developed to some extent there. They have established factories; they have not done much with their electrical power for the farmers, but they have done well, they have an immense store of electrical energy in Quebec, and they can use that for the control of these railway rates. With electrical energy developed from the rivers of Quebec, every railroad running from the Ottawa river down to the Maritime Provinces can be run and, perhaps, at a lower cost than with coal produced in the Maritime Provinces. If you are looking for the cheapest possible transportation and you can get it by water-power, why not have it?
It is rather an unusal thing, after hearing all that we have heard about transportation in the United States, to have someone tell this House that corporation-owned railways in the United States have failed; but they failed and corporation-owned railways in Canada have failed likewise. The railways in the United States are not publicly-owned, whereas, our national railways are, and we are going to keep them. We are going to try them out to see what relief they will give to the people of this country, and we are going to keep Sir Adam Beck where he is generating hydro-electrical power in Ontario for the benefit of the people.
I regret that the organized farmers of Ontario have started out to crucify Sir Adam Beck because he is generating tremendous quantities of electrical power in that province for the service of the people. I do not say that hon. gentlemen here take that view of the matter; but that is largely the direction in which the discussion is going in Ontario to-day, where there is a man who has surpassed the President of the United States in generating an immense quantity of water-power for purposes of transportation. I hope
The Address

hon. gentlemen from the West, and especially the new western members-we have all free transportation on the railways-will some Saturday or even some Sunday visit Niagara Falls and see the Chippewa electrical development plant that Sir Adam Beck has built on the Niagara river right at the falls. They will see the greatest triumph of Canadian engineering, surpassing anything ever before achieved by any engineers in the world in the way of electrical development. The generators were made in Toronto and the work was done largely by Canadian workmen. We have that electrical development in the province of Ontario, and at the very time of its arriving and its going to make good, there is a sudden and suspicious movement developing in this country, a movement directed mainly by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, threatening us and threatening the people of Canada. If you go into the ownership of railroads for your relief, have a care; we will see after you! That is the menace in this country. Not only has there been failure in the United States and failure in Canada, and great loss of money in railroads, but we are being told in the most defiant way that we must not indulge in public ownership. Hands off! Leave it to us! We will save it! I do not think they will.
I want to take up the question of what we can do to solve the transportation problem that faces us; and if you, Mr. Speaker, will call it six o'clock, and the House will give me half an hour after recess, I will go into that matter then.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before the House rose at six o'clock I was about to deal with a question that has come up in this House and in the press in connection with transportation, namely, the farmers' grievance respecting marketing. This matter was referred to by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) this afternoon, and I desire to make it clear, if possible, or at least to throw some light on the question. Now, the farmers of Canada as well as the farmers of the United States have a substantial grievance in connection with transportation. They complain, among other things, that when they have pretty

well got rid of their grain the price advances, and they want to sell at the higher rather than at the lower price. Some of the farmers here have been led to believe that the railway charges were the main cause of this loss to them. The farmer will certainly get relief from transportation charges, but he will get that relief in the way suggested by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and that is by adopting the plan that is followed in the United States. There is a very appropriate expression current in the United States in regard to marketing, and that is the phrase "orderly marketing." Now what does that mean? It means, largely, just what we had in this country in connection with the Wheat Board, which was undoubtedly successful in its operation during the war. That board kept prices pretty well up, and all the grain was sold and the money pooled, and when the season was over the proceeds were fairly divided; and flour and milling companies who had filled their elevators when the market was low were not able to take advantage of the condition of the market, nor were the speculators in a position to do so. Some system like that, and in accordance with the plan now in effect in the way of orderly marketing in the United States, should be followed here. That orderly marketing will have to be backed in Canada, as it has been backed in the United States, by the credit of the Government. We require two things; better railway management, or, in other words, national ownership of railways; and government credit behind some system of orderly marketing of grain and live stock products.
I shall now deal with the question which I was considering before dinner, as to what the Government ought to do at the present time. They have told us that they intend to co-ordinate the railways. Now, what do they mean by co-ordination? Do they mean consolidation, and all that that signifies, as mentioned by the leader of the Progressive party? Or does co-ordination, as the Government uses the word, mean that the Canadian National system, comprising the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk, the Transcontinental, and other roads, is to be operated as five different systems, with five presidents, five executives, and, as in some places, like Vancouver, for instance, with two sets of stations, entailing a large expense? How does my hon. friend from Marquette construe the word "co-ordination " in this connec-

The Address
tion? When he used the word, did he mean the separate management I have just suggested, or did he mean amalgamation, with the economies resultant therefrom? This would go a long way in the direction of reducing traffic charges, which is exactly what the people want. Is that what he means?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Certainly, that is what
I mean.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: If that is also the Prime Minister's meaning I will accept it. I do not ask him to say whether or not he means that, but that is the issue before the people of Canada to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: When the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) gives his statement to the House he will make quite clear what is meant in this respect. In the meantime, if it will help to clear my hon. friend's mind, I may say that it is the intention of the Government to have one board of directors that will manage the entire system in a manner that will effect economies and further efficiency very much in accord with what he has in view.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend means just what he says. If not, there will be an opportunity later on to move an amendment-we have lots of opportunities to submit amendments; I have been under the impression that we were limited to one amendment in this debate, but that is not so, it is on going into Supply that we are limited to one amendment. Now, notwithstanding what any of us may say as regards the interpretation of the word "co-ordination," we have the statutes of Canada to which we may turn. Here is Chapter 13 of 1919, the Act Incorporating the Canadian National Railway Company. That Act was passed mainly on the strength of our taking over the Canadian Northern and in view of the fact that we had the Intercolonial and other Government roads, and in sections 11 and 12 it clearly sets out what the Government can do. So that it does not require any considerable inquiry to find out what ought to be done in this respect; the man who assumes the responsibility of carrying on the government of this country must be ready to act, even though he cannot obtain counsel outside. It is all very well to make1 inquiries, and probably the leader of the House is within his rights in making full investigation; and the last Government was quoted in that respect this afternoon in connection with the tariff; but the best way to deal with a question is to
deal with it. The Greeks had a very good proverb: to the effect that to play upon the lyre or the harp you must play upon it. So, to deal with this railway question you do not have to make an inquiry so much as you have to consolidate the railways. You might make inquiries that would last until doomsday and not get anywhere. The Prime Minister has taken a responsible position in this country, just as my hon. friend from Marquette has assumed the responsibility of leading a party in this House; and I want to tell that hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) without being at all offensive, what I think of his position. He is the leader of a party in this House, the leader of an opposition, and apparently he has contracted himself, in a way, out of the liability of the recognized leader of the Opposition. Here is a new precedent: Parliament has for the first time recognized by statute the position of leader of the Opposition. Heretofore the leader of the Opposition had a recognized status both in British and in Canadian politics, a status defined not by legislation but by convention. At any rate, I do not like the idea of anybody in this House escaping a responsibility, especially if he is a leader of an opposition. The responsibility is on him just as it is on the Prime Minister to find out what ought to be done with regard to such questions as the consolidation of the railways of this country. I have defined my position, and I hope to get a clear statement from the Minister of Railways, when we hear from him, as to what is proposed to be done. We want more light on this thing. I sincerely hope that before this debate concludes there will be a response to our insistence upon knowing what is meant by this promise of co-ordination and what the Government intends to do with regard to the statute passed by Parliament two years ago providing for these very things. The duty of the Government is not to get behind some inquiry which they may propose to make; it is to carry out this statute or amend it so that this necessary consolidation may be effected.	.
Now, I am going to pass from that to a summary of what I think the Government ought to do. First, of course, they ought to consolidate the railways. The next thing they ought to do-it has never been done in this country, but if it is not done we shall find ourselves where the President of the United States has landed and where the farmers of the United States have landed-is to make the railway services
The Address

complementary of the water services of the country so that the two will work together. In the United States they have practically murdered water competition; they have bought up all the steamboat lines and all the wharves; they have put the steamship lines out of business. One paper, from which I read this afternoon and which apologizes for the conditions with respect to railways, expresses regret that the boats have gone out of business. At great cost we have built up a system of government ships; the services carried on by these must be made complementary of our railway services and of our other waterway systems. We may have to establish seaports on the lakes as far up as Port Arthur, if necessary, in order to bring about a solution of this transportation problem. Some years ago, after a good deal of agitation in which I myself took some little part, the railways were compelled to reduce their freight rates, but their friends the steamship companies had effected a combine and no sooner were the railways forced to reduce their rates than the steamship lines put on a corresponding increase. To effect consolidation you must make the canals, the railway, the inland water services, and the ocean-going steamship services, complementary one of the other. If you are canalizing the rivers and improving the lakes you must let the steamships get up into lake Superior. Electrification of the railways is absolutely necessary, and must be controlled and maintained by the people as a public service. The proposal is to spend hundreds of millions upon this international waterway scheme; let us, therefore, keep it in the people's hands. We want to back up Sir Adam Beck in what he is doing in Ontario in the development of water-powers.
I want to tell my hon. friend the Prime Minister what I think his Minister of Railways ought to do, right away, toward consolidation. A reference to the time table of the Canadian National Railways will show that the different lines are all mapped therein-Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk Pacific, Transcontinental, Intercolonial and other roads. If you look at the map you will see where the Canadian Northern runs northwesterly from lower Ontario to lake Nipigon. At Long lake, which is thirty miles from the Transcontinental, the line dips down in a southwesterly direction and proceeds to Port Arthur and Fort William. Now, if the Minister really wants to effect this consolidation, this amalgamation, let

him come down to the House and tell hon. gentlemen from the West that nobody is going to stop him from building this projected thirty miles and shortening the distance by one hundred miles between Manitoba and points east. Do you know that the Act to which I have referred enables the Minister of Railways of his own motion to have this thirty miles built and to improve the grades? The great feature of the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern is the improvement effected in the grades; they are away ahead of the old Grand Trunk and of the Canadian Pacific.
I wish just here to make some further reference to a point I mentioned this afternoon with regard to grades. Toronto is a great railway centre. A large part of the traffic of the Grand Trunk originates in Chicago and must pass through Toronto, and it all has to go over a one per cent grade from Scarborough. The same applies to the Canadian Pacific. The Minister of Railways has engineers available who have made surveys; their draughtsmen have plans for the changing of that one per cent grade in Toronto, of the Canadian Pacific as well as of the Grand Trunk, to a half per cent grade. I was speaking the other day to Mr. McGuigan, who is an authority on Grand Trunk affairs, and he said:	If we had that reduction of grade,
as I told the late Mr. Hays, we would do with one engine and two men what now requires eight engines and sixteen men. Now that can be effected in the city of Toronto. And if the Minister of Railways cannot get the information in his department, and cares to ask me, I think I can show him how effective that one thing would be in helping to solve the transportation difficulties of this country. My proposal would be a temporary one, just for the time being, but it could be put in operation within eight weeks. There are four miles of a double track in a level country, but there is a long wooden trestle to be built, at no great cost, and if this were built it would effect a saving that would mean hundreds of thousands of dollars in the reduction of freight rates on traffic that goes through Toronto alone. There are cases like that all over the country. As the Century Magazine said, you have two stations in Vancouver, and another one for an American road, when half a station would be enough for all the railroad business of that territory. Think of it '*-three railway stations and three equipments to do the railway business of

The Address
Vancouver. This American magazine, after speaking of this Vancouver duplication, says, "Do not think we have not got any duplication in the United States," and then it goes on to speak of duplication in the city of Spokane and all over the United States. We have duplication all over this country that makes you sick when you see it; we have station after station duplicated, at great expense, and line after line that could be cut out or a substitute put in that would give better service for half the money. Economies can be effected all over. Are these economies to be effected by hon. gentlemen opposite? 

and I ask that with all respect. They have been the apostles of economy in this country. Let me tell them a story about an election speech down in Glengarry. There was a candidate there, Mr. Rory McLennan-I remember when he sat in this House. A lawyer got up to make a speech for Rory. He said, "We have a fine candidate in Mr. Rory McLennan. We all think a lot of him. There is not one of us would not take off his coat and fight for him." A Highland Scotchman in the audience, hearing that, ran down the aisle and taking off his coat shouted, "Here, Mister, now's your chance." I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, "Now's your chance." If you want to effect economies you can build this cut-off of thirty miles at Long lake, and the little cut-off I have spoken of at Toronto, as a start. I hope we shall hear from the Minister of Railways about these matters when he rises to speak, but in the meantime I say, now is the time to consolidate the railways. And not the railways only, for remember we have gone a long way further than that in the matter of public ownership. We have now not only the national railways, but we have a system of national telegraphs, for which we have paid dearly, but it is a fine system nevertheless; we have also got a national money order system, a national express system, and a national postal system. All these services can be co-ordinated and great improvements made in them right away. Get all these services together, and then go to the people of Canada and say: Boys, we have a national telegraph company; let us see that our people use it; we have a national money order system, and a national system of express, let us see that our people use that. That is what the people want to hear when this railway question is up. That is what the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the gentlemen behind him must insist
on if they want relief in the matter of freight charges.
There is another thing, and now I wish to appeal especially to the West. Now that you have got national railways, national telegraphs, national express, and a national money order business, and you have them all now in every station in the West as we have in the East, consolidate them in one building and make them the centre of the community. If you want to work out your own salvation, build, at your own expense if you have to, a little community centre large enough for the village or town or city and use that for the service of the public. Put these services in there. Perhaps you could also put a drug service in there too..

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do not
mean the kind hon. gentlemen have in mind. The war is over and regeneration must take place in this country the same as everywhere else, and you can begin regeneration with a local centre, and the way to do it is to get all these services together in one building. You can do a lot of things like that in the West. Just put up one little building as the community centre, and invite the Government to put the national express, the national telegraph, the national money order and railway business there, and let the postmaster go after the freight and see that the national railways get it, as well as their share of the telegraph and express business.
There is something else that can be done. You can back up the good roads, and make the good roads in your respective provinces complementary of the national system of transportation. What has thrown the American railroads into consternation more than anything else is the competition of the good roads and the motor truck. The railways of the United States are deploring the fact that the competition of the good roads and the motor truck has almost put them out of business. The motor truck travelling over the good roads has this marvellous advantage over the railways, that for short distances it is a handling of freight and passengers from door to door, with no intervening cartage agent, or street car journey, or anything of that kind. The motor truck goes from door to door and is playing the very dickens with the American system of railways. They do not know how to meet this competition, and they may have to go into a receivership for
The Address

that reason alone. We must consolidate our railway service with all these other services if we want to get improved transportation, and I hope that we are going to get something of that kind now, but the beginning of it must be action on the part of the Government and our demand in this House for that action.
I have practically closed the argument that I have endeavoured to present to the House this afternoon, namely, that the fundamental problem in the regeneration of our country to-day, after the great war, is the improvement of our transportation to bring relief to our people who are so anxiously seeking it in that direction. And there is a way to do it, now that we own five of the railways, now that we own steamships, and now that we own telegraph and express services. But we have to go after the business; we have got to canvass for business just the same as the privately owned railways do. And that is what the Canadian Pacifi.c Railway Company fears will happen. As I said I have no grievance against the Canadian Pacific railway except this-that it will not solve the transportation problem for us. As a private corporation it cannot do that; and we are not going to allow them to try, notwithstanding the advice of the Montreal Gazette. Within the past week the Montreal Gazette has told the Government to get rid of these national railways1-put them on the scrap heap or give them away. Is that the view of the people of Canada or of the members of this House? I do not think so. We are going to try and work out some improvement, and we expect that improvement to come from the new Government following uip legislation already on the statute books. We will expect it most of all from the new Minister of Railways; and we will be only too glad to welcome the fact that the Government, now that the opportunity has come to it, is going to consolidate all these railroads and steamships that we now possess in order to secure lower traffic charges in Canada.
Just one word more. Much was said in the speeches of yesterday-and they were good speeches-but I think the leader of the Progressives, in the effort he made this afternoon, endeavoured to bring the situation right home to the people and to the members of the House. It is a fine thing to make an exhibition of swordsmanship such as we had yesterday between the two leaders, a fine thing to make the respective groups of followers cheer, but that is not dealing with

public questions. We want these questions taken up and dealt with from the transportation point of view. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) endeavoured to do that this afternoon, and in my humble way I have followed in the same direction, and I am going to try and do a little more later on. As I have already stated, during my election campaign the electors indicated their preference for a discussion of the transportation question and the subject of the consolidation of our railroads. We have these railroads now and it is our duty to make a success of them as far as we can. I want to tell the leader of the Government that there is a newspaper in Toronto called the Globe and it is taking up these questions, while Montreal papers such as the Gazette and the Star are talking in an altogether different way. The people all over Ontario are thinking in terms of public ownership, but a large number of the newspapers of this country are passing away from public ownership, and are supporting corporation ownership of our railways. Such a policy as that will not succeed.
Before resuming my seat I must apologise to hon. members for the time I have occupied, but I have spoken at length in order to ventilate what I deem to be a more important view of the transportation questions of Canada than has hitherto been expressed.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I fully appreciate the privilege accorded to me of having the opportunity to address the House at this particular time. I highly appreciate the dignity and importance of this, the Parliament of Canada, and I only hope that I may be able, in my small way, to maintain its past traditions and that I may be found worthy of the place which I occupy in this Chamber.
In commencing I desire to compliment you, Mr. Speaker, on your elevation to the commanding position of First Commoner. Your high character and great attainments as a public man are not unknown even in the remotest parts of this great Dominion of ours, and I am sure that you will brilliantly adorn the high position to which you have been promoted. I listened with a great deal of attention yesterday to the excellent speeches of the Mover and Seconder of the Address. I must compliment Mr. McMurray, who belongs to the same province as myself, upon the ability which characterized his speech, and I am sure that he fully maintained the reputation

The Address
which he enjoys in the west as a public speaker.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am sorry to have transgressed the rules. I should have alluded to my hon. friend as the hon. member for North Winnipeg. Perhaps it would be only right for me to say that I am a new member and therefore unfamiliar with the procedure of this House. For that reason I would ask the indulgence of hon. members, and I can assure them that I will endeavour as quickly as I can to conform to Parliamentary methods and usages.
I was sorry that I was unable to follow the speech of the hon. member who seconded the Address. I have, however, read a short synopsis of that speech translated into English and have therefore familiarized myself to a certain extent with the views which he expressed. From the style of his speech and the sentiments which he uttered I should deem him to be an eloquent and able speaker. It is a matter of deep regret to me that I am unable to understand the French language. Let me say that were I a young man nothing would give me greater pleasure than to begin the study of that tongue and to acquire such a mastery of it as would enable me to follow the speeches of hon. members from Quebec when they use the language of old France.
I listened with a great deal of attention to the speeches that were made yesterday by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The former has certainly lost none of his old-time ability, and he can still drive with rapier-like thrusts at the enemy across the way. I am one of those who admire the ability of the right hon. member. He is a dweller in our province, and although we do not agree with his political opinions we are proud of his ability and glad to see him once more in Parliament.
I read very carefully the Speech from the Throne, and I was glad to observe that a good many of the things for which we have been hoping were promised therein. I trust the promises will come to fruition and that some day we shall reap the harvest that has been sown. For one thing we have been promised wider markets. The leader of the Opposition yesterday in his speech ridiculed the idea of reciprocity with the United States. I am sorry to observe that attitude on his part because in the West it is something unusual to find such a brand of opinion-as will be recognized from what happened there during
the recent elections. I can assure the House that one of the great problems that we have to meet in the West to-day is the getting of wider markets for farm products. The question has been asked:	Of what
advantage would the United States markets be to the western farmer? Let me tell the House that last fall and during the early part of the winter, notwithstanding the emergency tariff, trainload after trainload of cattle left the St. Boniface stock yards, paid the American duty of 30 per cent and were taken to Chicago and St. Paul and there sold at a profit over what those cattle could have realized at Winnipeg. What would have happened had there been no outlet for that trade, with the cattle market in such a depressed condition? Had there been no market in the country to the south to take our surplus at that particular time our cattle would have been unsaleable during those fall months. So that, you see, even with the 30 per cent duty, that American market at the present time has been a great advantage to us in respect to the marketing of our cattle.
Then we have a mention of freight rates in the Speech from the Throne, and with this I shall deal a little later on. We need relief in that respect. I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speech of the hon. member, (Mr. Maclean, York) who preceded me. I should like to tell him that I am in thorough accord with him as far as the consolidation of the National railways is concerned, and I think he will get the support of this portion of the House in that policy. I am a new member of this Chamber, and do not know the position of the different members in the House very well yet, but I could not help wondering to what division the hon. gentleman who has just spoken belongs.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am a public rights man, and I hope you are too.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH. ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I intend, to be, and I say so, with all due respect to the remarks the hon. gentleman has made, and I do not say it in any carping or criticising spirit. Some reference was made in the Speech from the Throne to the tariff. I agree with the leader of the Opposition, the right hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Meighen) in some of the criticisms he made in this respect. The reference to the tariff in the Speech may mean a great deal or it may mean very little. I have an optimistic temperament, and I have no doubt the Government will implement its promises,
The Address

and that we are to have substantial reductions in the tariff, more especially in the matter of agricultural implements and the materials we need in agriculture. If we do not get relief in this way, there is going to be disappointment in the West, and, more than that, there is going to be disaster unless some remedy is brought forward to meet conditions as they exist at the present time. The prairie provinces are in need of immediate relief; the situation out there is not good, and no one can face the circumstances without realizing that some relief must be afforded. We are aware of the fact that the climatic conditions have been unfavourable for a number of years, but anyone who knows the situation will realize that the overhead expenses of agriculture at the present time are far and away out of all proportion to the va}ue of the crops that are being harvested. Now, that sort of thing cannot continue; it must come to an end; you cannot carry on business year after year if the balance is on the wrong side of the ledger. Something will have to be done to remedy those conditions. The prosperity of these provinces depends entirely upon their natural resources, and the greatest of those natural resources is that three or four inches or more of fertile soil that covers the land from eastern Manitoba to the foot of the Rocky Mountains.
